explanation:
The 'override' specifier, introduced in C++11, is a contextual keyword used to explicitly state that a member function in a derived class is intended to override a virtual function from a base class. It serves as a contract with the compiler, ensuring that your intent to override is validated at compile time, preventing a class of common and subtle bugs in polymorphic hierarchies.

Scott Meyers emphasizes that virtual function overriding is deceptively error-prone. Subtle signature mismatches—such as differing const-ness, parameter types (e.g., int vs. unsigned int), or reference qualifiers—can result in the derived class function *hiding* or *overloading* the base function rather than overriding it. Since this often compiles without warnings, it can lead to silent, hard-to-debug polymorphic bugs. The 'override' specifier is the definitive solution to this problem, turning these potential logic errors into clear compiler errors.

The mechanics are straightforward: when you append 'override' to a member function declaration in a derived class, the compiler performs a check. It verifies that an accessible base class exists which contains a virtual function with an identical signature, which includes the function name, parameter types, const/volatile qualifiers, and reference qualifiers. If no such function exists to be overridden, the compiler issues an error. This check also validates that the base function was actually declared virtual in the first place.

In practice, this means you should mark every single overriding function in a derived class with 'override'. It makes the code clearer by documenting intent and makes maintenance far more robust. If a base class virtual function's signature is refactored, the 'override' specifier ensures that all derived classes will fail to compile until they are updated accordingly, preventing the codebase from silently breaking and guiding the developer to the exact locations needing attention.

The most common and dangerous pitfall is simply omitting 'override'. Without it, a programmer might accidentally create a new virtual function in the derived class instead of an override, breaking the polymorphic behavior of the class hierarchy. This leads to unexpected behavior where calls through a base class pointer execute the base implementation instead of the intended derived one, a bug that can be extremely difficult to track down.
practical_example: When refactoring a large class hierarchy, changing the signature of a base class virtual function could silently break polymorphism in dozens of derived classes. Using 'override' on all derived functions turns this into a manageable task, as the compiler will provide a precise list of every location that needs to be updated.
keywords: override specifier, C++ virtual override, override keyword, C++11 override
